clauses.reason: Terminated by its own terms at the end of the Eighty-sixth Congress. Executive Order 10855, signed November 27, 1959 (24 FR 9565, PDF pages 7-7), orders that income tax (years 1945 to 1958, inclusive, as the order first read; Executive Order 10876 later changed the closing year to 1959) returns shall, during the Eighty-sixth Congress, be open to inspection by the Senate Committee on the Judiciary, or any duly authorized subcommittee, in connection with its study and investigation of the applicability of the antitrust and anti-monopoly laws of the United States to professional boxing, pursuant to Senate Resolution 57, 86th Congress, agreed to February 2, 1959. The order sets no other term, condition or revocation clause. The terms of the Members of the Eighty-sixth Congress ended at noon on January 3, 1961 under the Twentieth Amendment, so the grant lapsed no later than that day; recorded as 1961-01-03 inclusive, with the exclusive reading (end when that day begins) disclosed as the alternative. The end source is the order's own operative text. Later event: see the later_events entry, which amends the paragraph but leaves the Congress limit unchanged.

research_rationale:
Identity: the registered original is the Federal Register printing of Executive Order 10855 (24 FR 9565, PDF pages 7-7; Federal Register issue of December 1, 1959; govinfo PDF text layer held at jobs/fr-originals/data/full_run/texts/EO_10855.txt), headed Executive Order 10855, signed by Dwight D. Eisenhower on November 27, 1959. The census register gives the same number, date and subject (Inspection of Income Tax Returns by the Senate Committee on the Judiciary). The text is an official scan read through its machine text layer; I read it for OCR damage and note below where damage matters. Inventory: the order is one grant, a single sentence opening income tax (years 1945 to 1958, inclusive, as the order first read; Executive Order 10876 later changed the closing year to 1959) returns to inspection by the Senate Committee on the Judiciary or any duly authorized subcommittee, followed by a sentence fixing its effective date on filing for publication. The grant is limited by its own words to the period of the Eighty-sixth Congress, which I treat as the order's fixed term. The terms of the Members of the Eighty-sixth Congress began at noon on January 3, 1959 and ended at noon on January 3, 1961 (Twentieth Amendment, sections 1 and 2). The Constitution is not among the held texts and no held source states that date, so the end date rests on that constitutional text together with the order's own words; no other source is claimed for it. First end: January 3, 1961 by the order's own terms, recorded inclusive. The exclusive reading (the end when that day begins) is the alternative the owner ruling requires me to disclose, but it fits poorly here because the Congress's terms ran until noon of that day. Later event: Executive Order 10876, signed April 22, 1960 (25 FR 3569), amends the first paragraph of this order by deleting the years 1945 to 1958 and inserting 1945 to 1959, and by inserting a reference to Senate Resolution 238, 86th Congress, agreed to February 8, 1960; it takes effect on filing for publication, and its Register filing line gives April 25, 1960. This is a strike-and-insert amendment, so the clause continues, amended, and the amendment does not touch the Eighty-sixth Congress limit; the owner ruling of 2026-10-21 on strike-and-insert amendments is applied. The dossier's two leads for Executive Orders 10850 and 10854 (cited by number, no change provision located) are held Register page texts that print this order's heading on a shared page with those neighbouring orders; they do not change it. The three chosen machine searches state their coverage with no warning and their coverage notes were read. The U.S. Code and eCFR searches returned no hit for this order; the later-events search returned the hits recorded as Executive Order 10876 (the amendment recorded as a later event below) and no other change.

savings.reason: The order contains no savings, exception or transitional clause; I read its whole text for such wording. Any inspection made while the grant ran is a completed act, and nothing in the order continues the grant after the Eighty-sixth Congress ended. Any later statutory change to the Internal Revenue Code sections the order cites would postdate this end and cannot be a first end.
